subtype: Approach: supporting a grieving family member [Action]
passage: I'm Zubin, Shankar's friend from the next building, and I drop off his notes each evening at six. It's always the same scene. Shankar is on the balcony steps with his mother, who lost his father in June. He brings her tea before she asks. Mostly they sit. Sometimes she talks about their wedding trip, about how his father hated onions, and Shankar just listens, nodding. Once I heard a visitor say from the doorway, “Time heals everything,” and saw her face tighten. Shankar never says that. He says “hmm” or “tell me more.” I can't tell what is going on in his head. He looks tired. But whenever I leave, her hand is on his arm.

qa.q: What does Shankar bring his mother before she asks?
qa.a: Shankar brings her tea before she asks.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother have felt when the visitor said time heals everything?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or unheard, since her face tightened at the words.

qa.q: What could Shankar do if his mother stops talking altogether?
qa.a: Shankar could keep sitting with her and offering presence, and ask a relative or counsellor to help if she seems overwhelmed.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother see the evenings on the steps?
qa.a: She probably feels comforted, since Shankar sits, listens and lets her keep a hand on his arm. 🤍

grounding: A teen sits quietly with his widowed mother in the evenings, offers tea and listens, avoiding empty phrases, as seen by a friend.

subtype: Approach: supporting a grieving family member [Action]
passage:
First evening after the thirteenth-day ceremony. The relatives had gone. Sameer found his mother, Tanuja, sitting on the balcony in the dark. He wanted to say something wise. Everything he thought of, "He's in a better place," "Be strong, Mummy," sounded hollow. So he made two cups of tea and sat beside her. They didn't talk.
A week later. Same balcony. This time she spoke first, about how Papa used to burn the toast every Sunday. Sameer just listened, and laughed when she laughed. When she cried, he didn't try to stop it. He passed her the dupatta she'd dropped.
A month later. His aunt Mahima phoned, asking if Tanuja was "over the worst." Sameer glanced at the balcony, where two cups already waited. "She's still sad," he said. "We sit together in the evenings. That helps."

qa.q: What did Papa use to burn every Sunday?
qa.a: Papa used to burn the toast every Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Sameer stay silent on the first evening?
qa.a: Sameer wanted to comfort his mother but felt every phrase sounded hollow, so he chose quiet company over empty words.

qa.q: What else could Sameer do on harder evenings?
qa.a: Sameer could gently ask whether she wants to talk or just sit, and let Mahima or another adult share some evenings, so he isn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How does Tanuja experience the evenings on the balcony?
qa.a: Tanuja has someone beside her who doesn't rush her grief, so she can remember Papa, laugh and cry freely.

grounding: Shows a teen sitting quietly with his widowed mother, bringing tea and listening without empty phrases, trusting presence over fixing her pain.

subtype: Approach: supporting a grieving family member [Action]
passage: Swati beti, you asked how to help your aunt now that her husband has gone. Let me tell you about my Faisal. When his abba died, Faisal was fourteen. The whole mohalla came with advice: "Be patient, Rehana," "Keep yourself busy," "Time heals." Everyone talked. Faisal didn't. Every evening after namaz he came to my room with two cups of chai and sat on the floor by my feet. Some nights I talked about his abba's silly rhymes. Some nights I only cried. He never said, "Don't cry, Ammi." Once I asked him, "Why don't you say anything?" He said, "I don't know what to say, so I'm just staying." That staying, beti, did more for me than all the advice in the mohalla put together.

qa.q: How old was Faisal when his abba died?
What was Faisal feeling when he said he didn't know what to say?
qa.a: Faisal felt unsure and helpless about finding the right words, but cared enough to keep coming every evening anyway.

qa.q: Which choice of Faisal's mattered most in the story, and why?
qa.a: Choosing to sit with his mother every evening with chai, without advice or telling her not to cry, because it let her talk or weep as she needed.

qa.q: How did Rehana experience the mohalla's advice compared with Faisal's presence?
qa.a: The advice felt like a lot of talk, while Faisal's quiet staying comforted her far more than all of it together.

grounding: Illustrates a teen supporting his widowed mother by sitting with her each evening with tea, listening and avoiding empty phrases.
